scenes.title: The ACT in 20 minutes
scenes.subtitle: + 3 quick wins
scenes.say: Hey everyone! I'm Astra, the AI tutor here at Aced. Welcome to our very first live lesson! Tonight we're covering the ACT in twenty minutes: how the test works, how it's scored, and three quick wins you can use right away. Drop your questions in the chat anytime. And when a practice question pops up, type your answer in the chat before I reveal it. Let's see who gets it first! Ready? Let's light up some stars.

scenes.title: What's on the test
scenes.say: Let's start with the big picture. The ACT has three main sections, plus one optional one.

First, English. Fifty questions in thirty-five minutes. You'll read short passages and fix grammar, punctuation, and how ideas flow. Second, Math. Forty-five questions in fifty minutes. Algebra, functions, geometry, and some statistics. And yes, you can use a calculator. Third, Reading. Thirty-six questions in forty minutes. Four passages, and one of them is actually two short passages you compare. And then there's Science. Forty questions in forty minutes. Here's the thing most people don't know: Science is now optional. It's not about memorizing facts. It's about reading charts, tables, and experiments.

scenes.caption: 4 answer choices. Every question.
scenes.say: Every multiple choice question has four answer choices. Not five. Four. That's going to matter in a minute.

scenes.title: How it's scored
scenes.say: Now, scoring. Each section gets a score from one to thirty-six.
Your composite score, the big number colleges look at, is the average of three sections: English, Math, and Reading. Science gets its own separate score.
So if you get a twenty-four in English, a twenty-six in Math, and a twenty-five in Reading, add them up, that's seventy-five, divide by three, and your composite is twenty-five.

scenes.caption: Wrong answer = blank answer = 0 points. Guessing is free.
scenes.say: And here's the most important rule on the whole test. There is no penalty for guessing. A wrong answer and a blank answer count exactly the same. So never, ever leave a question blank. If you're out of time, pick a letter and fill in the rest.

scenes.question: 30 seconds left, 5 questions to go. What do you do?
scenes.answer: Fill in an answer for every one.
scenes.explain: A guess has a 1 in 4 chance. A blank has zero.
scenes.say: Quick check! In the chat: if you have thirty seconds left and five questions to go, what should you do?
scenes.sayAfter: Fill in an answer for every single one. Even a random guess gives you a one in four chance. A blank gives you zero.

scenes.say: Let's talk timing, because running out of time is the number one way students lose points. In English, you get about forty-two seconds per question. That's fast, but most English questions are quick. In Math, Reading, and Science, you get about one minute per question.

scenes.caption: Guess · mark it · move on.
scenes.sticky: One hard question shouldn't steal time from three easy ones.
scenes.say: Here's my pacing trick. If a question is taking you more than about a minute and a half, mark it, make your best guess, and move on. Come back at the end if you have time. Never let one hard question steal time from three easy ones.

scenes.title: Comma after an intro phrase
scenes.say: Okay, quick win number one. This is for English. When a sentence starts with an intro phrase, like 'After the game,' you put a comma right after that phrase.

scenes.title: Lift it out. Still a sentence?
scenes.check: "We got pizza." ✓ full sentence → use the comma
scenes.say: Here's the test. Lift the intro phrase out. If what's left is still a full sentence, use the comma. 'We got pizza.' Still a full sentence. So the comma goes in.

choices: Afterward we drew a plan.
Afterward, we drew a plan.
Afterward; we drew a plan.
Afterward: we drew a plan.
scenes.explain: Semicolons and colons need a full sentence before them.
scenes.say: Your turn! In the chat. Which is correct?
scenes.sayAfter: The answer is B! 'Afterward' is an intro word, so it gets a comma. And remember, semicolons and colons need a full sentence before them. 'Afterward' isn't a full sentence, so C and D are out.

choices: Running every morning, helps me focus.
Running every morning helps me focus.
Running, every morning helps me focus.
Running every morning; helps me focus.
scenes.explain: Lift out "Running every morning" → "helps me focus." Not a sentence, so no comma.
scenes.say: Here's a tricky one. Use the lift-out test. Which is correct?
scenes.sayAfter: It's B! Watch what happens when you lift out 'Running every morning.' You're left with 'helps me focus.' That's not a full sentence. 'Running every morning' isn't an intro phrase here. It's the subject. So no comma. The lift-out test tells you when to use a comma, and when not to.

scenes.caption: The answer is always right there.
scenes.say: Quick win number two. This one's for Math, and it's a lifesaver. On the ACT, the answer is always right there in the choices. So if you get stuck setting up an equation, just try the answer choices in the problem and see which one works.
Try this one in the chat. If three x plus five equals twenty, what is x?
scenes.sayAfter: It's B, five! You could solve it: subtract five to get three x equals fifteen, then divide by three. Or plug in: three times five is fifteen, plus five is twenty. It works. Pro tip: start with a middle answer choice. If it's too big, you know to go smaller. If it's too small, go bigger. You'll often find the answer in two tries.

scenes.work: Try B: 2(7) − 7 = 7 → too small ↑   Try C: 2(9) − 7 = 11 ✓
scenes.say: Let's practice starting in the middle. Two x minus seven equals eleven. What is x? Try plugging in, and put your answer in the chat.
scenes.sayAfter: It's C, nine! Start with B, seven. Two times seven is fourteen, minus seven is seven. That's too small, so go bigger. Try C, nine. Two times nine is eighteen, minus seven is eleven. That's it! Two tries, done.

scenes.big: If you can't point to it, don't pick it.
scenes.caption: The passage always proves the right answer.
scenes.say: Quick win number three. This is for Reading. The right answer is always backed up by the passage. Not by your opinion, and not by what sounds smart. If you can't point to the words in the passage that prove it, it's probably a trap.
So before you look at the choices, go back to the passage, find the lines, and predict the answer in your own words. Then pick the choice that matches your prediction.

scenes.title: Watch out for answers that are…
items: True, but don't answer the question
scenes.say: The trap answers usually do one of three things. They're too extreme, with words like 'always' or 'never.' They're true, but don't answer the question. Or they mix up details from different parts of the passage.

scenes.passage: Maya had practiced the solo for weeks. But when the spotlight hit her, her hands shook. She closed her eyes, counted to three, and began to play.
scenes.stem: Which choice is best supported by the passage?
choices: Maya had never played the solo before.
Maya was nervous when she started to perform.
Maya always gets stage fright.
Maya's solo was the best in the show.
scenes.explain: A is contradicted · C is too extreme · D is never said.
scenes.say: Your turn! Read this short passage. Which choice is best supported by the passage? Remember, if you can't point to it, don't pick it.
scenes.sayAfter: It's B! Point to the proof: 'her hands shook.' That shows she was nervous. A is wrong, because she practiced for weeks. C says 'always,' which is too extreme. And D is never mentioned at all. That's the trap answer that sounds nice but has no proof.

scenes.big: Read the chart, not your memory.
scenes.caption: Most Science answers are right there in the data.
scenes.say: Bonus round! Science time. Remember, Science on the ACT is mostly about reading data. You don't need to memorize facts. Most answers are sitting right there in the chart or table. Just find the pattern.

scenes.stem: Based on the table, about how much would a plant grow with 10 hours of light?
choices: 5 cm
7.5 cm
9 cm
12 cm
scenes.work: 10 hours is between 8 and 12 → growth is between 6 and 9 cm → 7.5 cm ✓
scenes.say: Look at this table. It shows how much a plant grows with different hours of light each day. Based on the table, about how much would a plant grow with ten hours of light? Answer in the chat!
scenes.sayAfter: It's B, seven and a half centimeters! Ten hours is right between eight and twelve. So the growth should be right between six and nine. That's seven and a half. No science facts needed. Just the table.

scenes.stem: 2 minutes left. 4 English questions to go. What's your best move?
choices: Spend it all on the first question
Leave them blank
Answer the quick ones, then guess on the rest
Go back and check old answers
scenes.explain: Never leave a blank, and don't let one question steal your time.
scenes.say: Last question of the night, and it puts everything together. You have two minutes left and four English questions to go. What's your best move?
scenes.sayAfter: It's C! Answer the quick ones first, then guess on the rest. Never leave a blank, and don't let one hard question steal time from the easy ones. Nice work, everyone!

scenes.title: Tonight's 5 stars
scenes.say: Let's put it all together. Know your timing. Never leave a blank. Use the comma lift-out test. Plug in the answer choices in Math. And in Reading, if you can't point to it, don't pick it. Every one of those is a skill on your Aced star map. Practice them, and you'll literally watch your stars get brighter.

scenes.title: See you next Sunday ✦
scenes.say: That's it for tonight! Quick recap: know your timing, use the comma test, and never leave a question blank, because there's no penalty for guessing. Head to your star map on Aced to see where you stand. And if you want to try the real thing, the Aced Mock Test is Saturday, December fifth. Next week, we're tackling commas. See you next Sunday!
